papers.title: HPV Oncogenes rewire DNA crosslink repair to create a PRIMPOL-dependent therapeutic vulnerability
papers.abstract: Cisplatin-based chemoradiation is the standard of care for both HPV-negative (HPV-) and HPV-positive (HPV+) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), even though patients with HPV+ tumors have better treatment responses and a better prognosis. Understanding how HPV status shapes this response could guide alternative strategies that lower long-term toxicity. Using genome-wide CRISPR screens, we show that the genetic requirements for surviving chemoradiation diverge between HPV- and HPV+ HNSCC cells. HPV+ cells tolerate cisplatin-induced interstrand crosslinks independently of the Fanconi anemia pathway, a phenotype recapitulated by expressing HPV16 E6 and E7 in an HPV-negative background. In these cells, DNA damage tolerance depends instead on PRIMPOL-mediated repriming and post-replicative gap filling by translesion synthesis polymerases. Although they recruit BRCA1 normally to double-strand breaks, BRCA1 accumulation at cisplatin-stalled forks is markedly reduced, indicating that BRCA1 function is uncoupled between these two substrates. This tolerance pathway leaves cells dependent on dynamic RAD51 turnover at single-stranded DNA gaps. Depletion of the RAD51 unloading factor FIRRM, or chemical stabilization of RAD51 filaments, selectively kills HPV+ and HPV oncogene-expressing cells treated with cisplatin, and PRIMPOL depletion rescues this lethality. Our findings show that HPV oncogenes rewire the response to crosslink-induced replication stress and identify RAD51 filament dynamics as a therapeutic vulnerability in HPV+ HNSCC.

papers.title: Versatile and Cross-Species Alveolar Type II Cell Isolation Using Humanized Monoclonal Antibody Upifitamab
papers.abstract: Alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells are primary adult alveolar stem cells that maintain healthy alveoli. AT2 cell dysfunction is broadly linked to many lung pathologies from emphysema to fibrosis. Isolation of AT2 cells with high purity is therefore central to diagnostic studies, proteomics, transcriptomics and ex vivo experiments that can lead to future AT2 cellular therapies. Current markers for AT2 isolation exhibit various limitations from species-restrictions (e.g., mouse vs human) to limited AT2 specificity, which creates challenges for flow cytometric gating/sorting and application to magnetic-activated cell isolation. While underrepresented in the literature, these bottlenecks have made AT2 cell isolation inherently difficult and slowed AT2 cell research. Here we leverage surface protein-restricted transcriptomics to identify the sodium phosphate transporter NaPi2b (SLC34A2) as a highly specific AT2 cell marker optimally detected with the humanized monoclonal antibody upifitamab. Upifitamab-based labeling of AT2 cells is compatible with flow cytometric or magnetic-activated AT2 isolation and applies to both mouse and human AT2 cells, thus streamlining protocols and circumventing species-specific nuances. AT2 cells obtained with upifitamab can be cultured as organoids, in monolayers or differentiated to AT1 cells. This simplified AT2 isolation approach should overcome several current barriers while facilitating ex vivo studies on alveolar biology and related therapeutic developments.

papers.title: Synthetic Hibernation Suppresses Osteosarcoma Growth and Protects Normal Tissue from Radiation
papers.abstract: Natural hibernation can arrest tumor growth, but whether this effect can be reproduced through repeated pharmacologically induced synthetic torpor (ST) remains unclear. It is also unknown whether the radioprotection conferred by natural and synthetic torpor extends to tumors, potentially compromising radiotherapy. Here, five 5 AMP induced torpor bouts administered every other day, a protocol designed to mimic repeated hibernation cycles (synthetic hibernation), markedly restrained osteosarcoma growth in female C3H/HeNRj mice bearing syngeneic LM8 tumors. Interestingly, growth suppression persisted long after the final torpor bout. When 6 Gy total-body X-ray irradiation was delivered during the second bout, tumor growth control was comparable with irradiation under normothermia, whereas ovarian follicular atresia was lower and remained similar to non-irradiated controls. Together, these findings support synthetic hibernation as a strategy to restrain tumor growth and mitigate normal-tissue radiation injury without compromising tumor control.

papers.title: A novel interaction between MNT and CCDC6: structural insights and distinct roles in cell migration and the DNA damage response
papers.abstract: MNT is a transcription factor of the MYC-MAX-MXD network whose biological functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify CCDC6, a tumor suppressor involved in the DNA damage response (DDR), as a novel MNT-interacting protein. Co-immunoprecipitation and interaction mapping analyses identified a part of the CCDC6 coiled-coil domain and the MNT bHLH-LZ region as major determinants of binding. Structural modelling further identified MNT residues predicted to mediate CCDC6 binding that are also critical for MNT-MAX dimerization. Transcriptomic analyses revealed substantial overlap between the gene expression programs regulated by MNT and CCDC6. Loss of either protein promoted cell migration, whereas MNT and CCDC6 cooperated in the regulation of {gamma}H2AX signalling, cisplatin responses and CCDC6 localization during the DDR. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized connection between CCDC6 and the MYC-MAX-MXD network through its interaction with MNT, revealing an additional layer of regulation within this transcriptional network.

papers.title: Haploidy-linked disruption of tissue organization in zebrafish larval eyes
papers.abstract: In vertebrate species, somatic haploidy generally causes embryonic or larval lethality with drastic morphological defects. However, the detrimental effects of haploidy at the cellular or tissue level remain largely unknown. In this study, we described cellular and tissue defects associated with haploidy in zebrafish larval eyes as a tissue model system. The haploid larval retina showed overall disorganized tissue layer structures. Photoreceptor cells, which usually align in the outermost tissue layer, were reduced in number and severely displaced, with drastic retardation of their connecting cilia and outer segments specifically in haploids. Ganglion cells in the inner retinal layer were also reduced in abundance and abnormally organized in haploids. These multifaceted cellular and tissue defects indicate that haploid eyes suffer severe visual functional defects, in addition to well-recognized size reductions. Our findings provide insight into diverse cellular principles that may limit the developmental capability of vertebrates in the haploid state.

papers.title: Reciprocal regulation of Wnt, receptor and Dvl localizations during cell polarization
papers.abstract: Migrating cells use multiple mechanisms to interpret signaling gradients and establish polarity. However, how non-migrating cells interpret such gradients remains poorly understood. In C. elegans, the polarity of asymmetrically dividing seam cells is redundantly regulated by three Wnt proteins: CWN-1, CWN-2, and EGL-20. Here, we show that these Wnts, their receptors, and Dishevelled (Dvl) proteins localize asymmetrically to the posterior side of seam cells in an interdependent manner. The receptors and Dvl colocalize in Wnt-dependent, membrane-associated puncta resembling signalosomes. These findings support positive-feedback mechanisms that links Wnt localization to cell polarity. Because posteriorly expressed CWN-1 and EGL-20 have instructive roles in seam cell polarity, this mechanism may help cells interpret their gradients. In contrast, despite its anterior expression, CWN-2 localizes posteriorly, suggesting that intrinsic polarity cues also contribute to Wnt localization. Together, these findings suggest that feedback integrates Wnt gradients with intrinsic polarity cues to robustly orient cell polarity.

papers.title: A Charcot-Marie-Tooth-associated dynamin mutation causes peripheral neuropathy-like phenotypes via Patronin/CAMSAP-dependent microtubule stabilization
papers.abstract: Dynamin-2 mutations are associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) neuropathy; however, how these mutations affect neuronal function in vivo remains unclear. Here, we generated a Drosophila model carrying a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of the shi549{Delta}3 mutation, corresponding to the human dynamin-2-551{Delta}3 variant, and examined its physiological and cellular consequences. The shi549{Delta}3 mutants exhibited progressive motor impairment across multiple genetic conditions. At the neuromuscular junction, the mutation caused synaptic overgrowth accompanied by excessive microtubule stabilization, including increased Futsch-positive loop structures and bouton numbers. Genetic interaction analysis revealed that reduction of Patronin, the Drosophila homolog of mammalian CAMSAPs, partially suppressed lethality and motor defects, linking microtubule stabilization to neuronal dysfunction in vivo. Consistently, CAMSAP2 knockdown in mammalian cells attenuated dynamin-2-induced microtubule acetylation, supporting a conserved mechanism. Together, these findings identify dysregulated microtubule stabilization as a key mechanism underlying neuropathy-like phenotypes caused by a CMT-associated dynamin mutation in vivo.

papers.title: Single-cell imaging links antibiotic resistance gene copy number and bacterial host identity
papers.abstract: Identifying the in situ microbial hosts of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in complex environments remains a major challenge, as many of these genes are associated with mobile genetic elements. Here, we introduce combined-FISH, which integrates direct-geneFISH for ARG detection with catalyzed reporter deposition fluorescence in situ hybridization (CARD-FISH) for rRNA labelling, thereby enabling the simultaneous visualization and copy number quantification of ARGs in taxonomically identified single cells within microbial samples. Using the sulfonamide resistance gene sul1 as a model target, we designed a polynucleotide probe set covering all non-redundant database sequences of this gene within 5% sequence mismatch. The method was validated using model organisms harboring plasmids with sul1, Escherichia coli K12 J53 with R388 and Acinetobacter defluvii with pOXA58_010030. Combined-FISH enabled quantitative determination of sul1 copy numbers at single-cell resolution, with E. coli harboring 1-8 copies and A. defluvii 1-4 copies per cell. Following plasmid-mediated transfer of sul1 from E. coli to Pseudomonas alloputida, recipient cells typically contained 2-6 sul1 copies, with up to 14 copies detected in individual cells, demonstrating the applicability of the approach for investigating horizontal gene transfer. The method was successfully applied to river biofilm samples containing sul1-harboring bacteria, enabling simultaneous tracking of the bacterial host and its associated ARG within a complex microbial community. Collectively, these results establish combined-FISH as a powerful tool for quantitatively linking ARGs and microbial hosts in situ, and for investigating plasmid copy number and gene transfer at single-cell resolution in technical and environmental systems.

papers.title: Brain proteinopathies associated physiological changes leading to cognitive resilience in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology has been well characterized, however the molecular mechanisms underlying resilience to the disease remain understudied. With the growing evidence of individuals who are resilient to AD and generation of cross-cohort multiomics data, it has become feasible to understand these mechanisms. In this study, we integrated longitudinal cognitive assessments, regional neuropathology, and matched prefrontal proteomic and metabolomic profiles across donors from two independent cohorts. We identified that asymptomatic AD (AsymAD) brains exhibited amyloid burdens comparable to AD but had fewer compact plaques, lower regional tau burden, and more restricted TDP-43 pathology. Across matched stages of amyloid, tau, and TDP-43 pathology, AsymAD was consistently distinguished from AD by preservation of mitochondrial translation and bioenergetics, synaptic programs, glutamatergic metabolites, and polyunsaturated membrane lipids. Longitudinal cognitive assessments further separated resilient from vulnerable AsymAD individuals despite comparable amyloid and TDP-43 burden, with vulnerability associated with greater neurofibrillary tangle accumulation. Both AsymAD groups retained a prefrontal proteome close to that of cognitively normal individuals, apart from amyloid-associated proteins, whereas mitochondrial, synaptic, and immune changes were largely confined to AD.

papers.title: Generalized inference of noise-corrected state variability in single cells
papers.abstract: Single-cell omics methods operate at their detection limit and are less conducive to technical controls than mini-bulk approaches, which combine cells of the same type before profiling. To integrate mini-bulk samples with paired split-pool controls more holistically, we built stochprofIC, an algorithm that considers data, noise, and covariates in a distributional-regression framework. We vet stochprofIC with synthetic datasets and compare against an adjusted-variance alternative using mini-bulk data in mouse brains and human breast cancers. The noise-batch corrections provided by stochprofIC enable inference of the single-cell populations comprising the mini-bulk, which are validated repeatedly by RNA FISH in different contexts. We use stochprofIC outputs as input to a systems model of nucleocytoplasmic transport and distinguish heterogeneous trafficking states. Pharmacologic inhibition of a MAP3K11-high state inhibits apoptosis in primary breast-cancer organoids, supporting relevance to phenotypes. By deconvolving changes in location and scale, stochprofIC supports mini-bulking when high-sensitivity and reliability profiles are important.

papers.title: Proton pump inhibitor-associated microbiomes shape systemic host responses
papers.abstract: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) consistently alter the gut microbiome, but the contribution of these changes to systemic effects associated with PPI use remains unclear. Here, we show that PPI-associated microbiome remodelling induces systemic metabolic and transcriptional responses independently of direct drug exposure. Integrating human microbiome and metabolomics data with metabolic modelling, we identified consistent alterations in microbial metabolic functions and host-microbiome co-metabolism. Transfer of PPI-associated microbiota into germ-free mice reproduced key metabolic changes observed in humans, particularly in aromatic amino acid metabolism, and induced additional alterations in systemic lipid metabolism. These changes were accompanied by tissue-specific transcriptional responses in the colon, liver and brain, affecting metabolic and inflammatory pathways. Together, our findings identify transferable metabolic and transcriptional microbiome-mediated signatures that may contribute to the adverse systemic effects associated with PPI use.

papers.title: RabA- and RabE-mediated trafficking define distinct branches of plant pre-invasive immunity
papers.abstract: Pre-invasive immunity constitutes a major barrier to disease and protects plants against the vast majority of filamentous fungal and oomycete pathogens through localized defence responses at sites of attempted invasion. Although membrane trafficking is essential for these responses, demonstrated by the requirement for the syntaxins PEN1 and SYP122, the underlying trafficking pathways remain poorly understood. Here, we show that trafficking mediated by the RabE and RabA GTPase subfamilies defines two functionally distinct branches of plant pre-invasive immunity. Inhibition of RabE rapidly compromised immunity to powdery mildew fungi, including the durable immunity conferred by mlo mutations, and reduced focal accumulation of PEN1 at papillae without substantially affecting callose deposition. By contrast, inhibition of RabA disrupted plasma membrane localization of multiple proteins and preferentially compromised immunity to the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans. Together, these findings support a model in which RabE promotes the powdery mildew-specific function of PEN1 in pre-invasive immunity, whereas RabA contributes to a broader defence pathway associated with the shared function of PEN1 and SYP122. Our results support a model in which pre-invasive immunity is coordinated by specialized trafficking modules with distinct pathogen requirements and establish RabA- and RabE-mediated trafficking as defining components of these pathways.

papers.title: Seed mycobiome assembly varies across mother trees with contrasting levels of resistance to Dutch elm disease
papers.abstract: Seed-associated fungal communities may influence plant performance from the earliest stages of development, yet their potential association with disease resistance in long-lived forest trees remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether Ulmus minor trees with different levels of resistance to Dutch elm disease (DED) exhibit consistent differences in their seed-associated mycobiome. We characterized the fungal communities inhabiting samaras from nine U. minor genotypes with different levels of DED resistance (i.e. resistant, intermediate and susceptible genotypes) using high-throughput sequencing of the internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS1) region. We identified 522 fungal amplicon sequence variants (ASVs), including 74 core members of the samara mycobiome. The community was dominated by Dothideomycetes and Tremellomycetes, but both diversity and community composition differed among resistance groups. Susceptible genotypes harbored richer fungal communities, whereas resistant genotypes supported less diverse but more distinct assemblages. Differential abundance analysis identified 21 genera associated with host resistance level, including an enrichment of Protofenestella in resistant genotypes and of Taphrina in intermediate and susceptible genotypes. Co-occurrence network analysis further revealed contrasting patterns of community organization, with resistant genotypes showing more modular and less connected networks than susceptible genotypes. Together, these findings indicate that DED resistance is associated with distinct patterns of seed mycobiome assembly, diversity and taxonomic composition in U. minor. The samara mycobiome may therefore represent a previously overlooked component associated with elm resistance, and provides candidate fungal taxa for future functional validation, with potential applications in elm conservation and mycobiome-informed breeding.

papers.title: Overcoming resistance to KRAS inhibition in KRAS/PIK3CA co-mutated colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Oncogenic alleles of KRAS drive colorectal cancers (CRC) growth and are associated with worse disease outcomes. Despite potent allele-specific and pan-RAS inhibitors targeting now in clinical test, CRC patients are not experiencing the same therapeutic benefit as patients with other cancers. PI3-Kinase (PI3K) is a direct RAS effector and is co-mutated in about 45% of CRC cases, raising the possibility that frequent oncogenic PI3K mutations contribute to the limited benefit of KRAS inhibition in CRC. Using isogenic colorectal cancer cells engineered to harbor either of the two most common activating PIK3CA mutations, we show that oncogenic PI3K promotes resistance to the pan-RAS inhibitor daraxonrasib (RMC-6236). Global phosphoproteomic profiling revealed that PIK3CA-mutant cells undergo a distinct adaptive response to RAS inhibition, characterized by sustained PI3K-AKT signaling and extensive remodeling of pathways controlling cell-cell adhesion and junction signaling, alongside suppression of apoptotic signaling. Combined RAS and PI3K inhibition overcame this resistance, suppressed signaling through both pathways and induced apoptosis in PIK3CA-mutant cells. Together, these findings identify oncogenic PIK3CA as a determinant of resistance to RAS inhibition in KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer and provide a mechanistic rationale for combined KRAS and PI3K inhibition in KRAS/PIK3CA co-mutant tumors.

papers.title: Loss of CDKN2A remodels Golgi morphology to create a lipid peroxidation vulnerability
papers.abstract: Loss of the tumor suppressor CDKN2A/p16 occurs in ~50% of human cancers, yet no therapies specifically target tumors with complete loss or reduced CDKN2A/p16 expression (hereafter CDKN2A/p16-Low). Identifying selective vulnerabilities in CDKN2A/p16-Low tumors therefore represents a critical unmet need. Here, we identify altered Golgi morphology as a vulnerability in CDKN2A/p16-Low melanoma. A CRISPR knockout screen revealed that genes associated with Golgi membranes are essential for CDKN2A/p16-Low cell survival. CDKN2A/p16 knockdown in human and murine cancer cells was associated with striking Golgi compaction. CDKN2A/p16 knockdown sensitized cells to pharmacologic Golgi disruption via lipid peroxidation both in vitro and in vivo. Notably, reduced Retinoblastoma-associated protein (RB1) expression did not recapitulate the increased sensitivity to Golgi disruption, supporting a role for non-canonical p16 functions in this vulnerability. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized link between CDKN2A/p16-Low status and Golgi remodeling, revealing a Golgi-associated metabolic vulnerability in CDKN2A/p16-Low melanomas.

papers.title: Deep Learning Identifies BMI-Associated Morphologic Features in Breast Cancer Tissue
papers.abstract: Multiple epidemiological studies have established obesity as an adverse factor in breast cancer incidence, progression, and clinical outcomes. However, the biological mechanisms underlying these associations remain incompletely understood. In peritumoral adipose tissue, obesity is associated with chronic inflammation, macrophage recruitment, and broader alterations in the local microenvironment. Whether these obesity-associated changes are accompanied by distinct morphologic features within the tumor and non-adipose stromal compartments remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether an AI-based pathology foundation model could support the development of machine learning algorithms capable of identifying obesity-associated morphologic patterns in histopathology images, with a particular focus on tumor and stromal regions. In a cohort of 195 patients with breast cancer, machine learning models using vector embeddings from non-adipose stromal regions classified high BMI ([≥]30 kg/m2) versus low BMI (<25 kg/m2) with an average AUC of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.73-0.83), consistently outperforming models based on tumor-only or combined tumor-stroma regions. These obesity-associated stromal signatures were observed across subgroups defined by hormone-receptor status and age, indicating that they are not restricted to specific clinical populations. Complementary embedding-based dissimilarity analysis further showed that higher BMI was associated with reduced inter-patient heterogeneity in both tumor and stromal tissues. Overall, these findings suggest that obesity is associated with distinct morphologic alterations in both tumor and non-adipose stromal tissues. Notably, the stromal compartment emerged as a particularly informative indicator of obesity-associated morphology and demonstrated reduced inter-patient heterogeneity among individuals with high BMI.

papers.title: Light power density governs local and systemic responses to photodynamic therapy
papers.abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a promising remedy against tumor cells by light activation of a photosensitizer, and its systemic antitumor effects are commonly attributed to immunogenic cell death and the release of soluble damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). Here, we show that light power density (mW/cm2), which is often treated as a mere technical parameter, determines whether PDT suppresses distant, unirradiated tumors. At an identical light dose (J/cm2), PDT at a low power density sustained singlet oxygen (1O2) generation in tumors, preserved tumor perfusion, and suppressed both irradiated and unirradiated tumors. PDT at a high power density resulted in reduced 1O2 generation, reduced tumor perfusion, and increased programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression in unirradiated tumors without inhibiting their growth. Serum levels of soluble DAMPs did not differ between the two conditions, whereas circulating small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) carried distinct protein cargo. Power density is thus a controllable determinant of the systemic effects of PDT, and circulating sEVs are candidate mediators of these effects.

papers.title: NPM1::ALK fusion-derived circular RNAs drive aggressiveness in ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma
papers.abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) derived from the NPM1::ALK fusion have been identified in ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALK+ ALCL), but their functional contribution to disease progression remains poorly understood. Divergent RT-PCR and long-read Nanopore sequencing identified eight NPM1::ALK-derived circRNA variants across ALK(+) ALCL cell-lines, a CRISPR/Cas9-engineered model, and a patient-derived xenograft. The abundance of f-circA23N2 and f-circA26N3, recurrently detected, steadily increased in crizotinib-resistant cell models. Both, highly stable, were predominantly cytoplasmic. Their overexpression in SU-DHL-1 did not affect NPM1::ALK expression, cell proliferation, or cell-cycle, in the absence or presence of crizotinib. circRNA overexpression delayed subcutaneous tumor-growth without altering response to crizotinib. Xenograft analysis disclosed altered immune response pathways and changes in inflammatory and myeloid-recruiting cytokines. RNA-seq deconvolution identified remodeling of the myeloid compartment. Intravenous f-circA23N2 and f-circA26N3 shortened survival with systemic lymphoma dissemination. NPM1::ALK-derived circRNAs appear to be non-cell-autonomous modulators of cytokine signaling and myeloid remodeling contributing to lymphoma dissemination.

papers.title: The SOX9 C-terminus encodes a transferable cBAF-recruitment module for enhancer remodeling and cell-state control
papers.abstract: Transcription factors select genomic targets, but how they recruit chromatin remodelers to convert DNA occupancy into cell-state-specific accessibility remains unclear. Here, we identify an intrinsically disordered SOX9 C-terminal module that recruits SMARCB1-containing canonical BAF (cBAF) to stem-like enhancers that open during APC-mutant adenoma formation. Acute, reversible SOX9 degradation displaces cBAF from ~80% of co-bound enhancers, exceeding effects on pBAF and ncBAF, and collapses accessibility and stem-like identity; SOX9 re-expression restores these features. C-terminal truncation preserves DNA binding but disrupts cBAF engagement and chromatin opening. Enforced SMARCB1 docking to truncated SOX9 partially restores cBAF recruitment, accessibility, stem-like transcription, and organoid self-renewal, identifying remodeler recruitment as a limiting effector function. The isolated C-terminus supports higher-order cBAF assembly and, when fused to dCas9 as COMET, redirects endogenous cBAF to targeted loci to open chromatin. Disordered TF regions can therefore encode transferable instructions that deploy specific remodeling complexes to control cell state.

papers.title: Reversible expression of a cartilage 'master regulator' during axolotl limb development and regeneration
papers.abstract: How the expression dynamics of cell fate transcription factors relate to emerging cell identities is not well understood. The axolotl limb is a powerful model for investigating the acquisition of cell fate: during development, the limb mesenchyme differentiates into multiple cell types; during regeneration, missing cell types are reconstituted. Here, we investigate the expression of SOX9, a transcription factor widely regarded as a ''master regulator'' of cartilage cell fate. By genetically fate mapping Sox9-expressing cells during development, we found that they give rise to two populations: cells that retain Sox9 expression and become cartilage or perichondrial cells, and cells that extinguish Sox9 expression and acquire alternative identities, such as dermal or interstitial fibroblasts. These populations differ in their contributions to regeneration: cells that retained Sox9 expression contribute little to skeletal regeneration, while cells that downregulated Sox9 contribute extensively, can reinitiate Sox9 expression and form new cartilage. We found that transiently Sox9-expressing cells are also present during early limb regeneration. Together, our findings link sustained or transient expression of a cartilage ''master regulator'' to distinct cell fates and subsequent contributions to skeletal regeneration.

papers.title: A novel mouse model recapitulates features of the neurodevelopmental disorder 3p25.3 microdeletion syndrome
papers.abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders globally affect approximately 15% of children and adolescents, but many disorders do not have mouse models, thus limiting our ability to further understand them and ultimately develop treatments. In our study, we developed a novel mouse line to model 3p25.3 microdeletion syndrome (6qE3del/+) that reliably recapitulates key features of the syndrome. 6qE3del/+ mice display congenital heart defects, craniofacial defects, skeletal anomalies and subtle brain changes. We also generated another neurodevelopmental disorder model for a gene often included in the deleted region, Brpf1, and found that congenital heart defects and craniofacial defects may be partly attributable to the heterozygous loss of Brpf1 in 6qE3del/+ mice. Together our work offers new neurodevelopment models, and provides evidence that treatments developed for Brpf1 haploinsufficiency may also benefit 3p25.3 microdeletion syndrome.

papers.title: Partial reprogramming reveals lineage-specific uncoupling of rejuvenation, function, and recoverability in human cells
papers.abstract: Partial reprogramming is therapeutically useful only if cells keep its benefits while recovering their lineage identity and function after the reprogramming factors are withdrawn. Whether the relationship between reprogramming depth and recovery differs between lineages is unknown. Using reversible, traceable Sendai-OSKM, we prospectively isolated intermediate reprogramming states from primary human fibroblasts, cytotoxic T cells, and aortic endothelial cells and followed their recovery. Outcomes diverged: fibroblasts kept a reduced DNA methylation age but retained stromal remodeling and incomplete proliferative recovery; T cells recovered only from shallow reprogramming, with enhanced effector function; endothelial cells rapidly recovered identity, kept a reduced methylation age, and markedly improved vascular function. None of this tracked iPSC derivation efficiency. Multiome and knockdown analyses identified TOX as a shared progression dependency, whereas its candidate downstream programs were predominantly lineage-specific. Partial reprogramming involves a lineage-specific tradeoff between rejuvenation and recovery that must be optimized one lineage at a time.

papers.title: Actin reorganization and junctional remodeling in podocyte foot process effacement
papers.abstract: Damage to podocytes results in kidney disease affecting millions of patients worldwide. Actin remodelling is a shared feature in podocyte FP effacement occurring after podocyte injury. However, it remains unclear which processes initiate and orchestrate cytoskeletal changes. Here, we show novel insights into actin dynamics during nephrotoxic serum nephritis and other podocyte disease models. Using Lifeact.mScarlet-I reporter expression and STED microscopy in podocytes, we could show distinct actin patterns occurring during FP effacement, independent of damage origin. Additionally, the protein composition of the slit diaphragm changed in a reversible manner. Tight junction proteins ZO-1 and Claudin-5 appeared at the plasma membrane with the onset of proteinuria. The changes in actin and junctional protein assembly during NTS nephritis were reversible as FP effacement disappeared, proteinuria declined and the podocytes recovered. For the first time, we could show with great spatial and temporal detail how the podocyte actin cytoskeleton adapts to insults and that a reversible response in slit diaphragm dynamics leads to a junctional remodelling better suited for upkeeping filtration barrier function.

papers.title: Defining a hypoxic exposure paradigm for modelling preeclampsia-associated syncytiotrophoblast dysfunction in human blastocyst-derived placental stem cells
papers.abstract: Introduction: Preeclampsia (PE) is a hypertensive pregnancy disorder in which placental dysfunction is thought to play a central role. Although hypoxia is widely used to model PE-associated syncytiotrophoblast (ST) dysfunction in vitro, considerable variability in oxygen control conditions and hypoxic exposure paradigms has limited standardization across studies. This study aimed to establish physiologically relevant oxygen control conditions and identify a hypoxic exposure paradigm that consistently recapitulates characteristic features of PE-associated ST dysfunction. Methods: Human blastocyst-derived trophoblast stem cells were differentiated into STs and exposed to physiological (8% O2), atmospheric (21% O2), or hypoxic (1% O2) conditions for 24 or 48 h. Angiogenic and apoptotic marker expression, cell death, and mitochondrial stress were assessed. Results: Compared with atmospheric oxygen, 8% O2 reduced cell death and more closely reflected physiological ST conditions. Acute hypoxia (24 h) induced a robust PE-like phenotype in STs characterized by induction of anti-angiogenic markers, sFlt-1 and sEng, reduced expression of the pro-angiogenic factor PlGF, and increased cell death, apoptotic signalling and mitochondrial stress. Notably, induction of several of these markers was attenuated or reversed following prolonged hypoxic exposure. Conclusions: These findings identify 8% O2 as a physiologically relevant control condition for modelling PE-associated ST dysfunction relative to 21% O2, and demonstrate that 24 h of severe hypoxia more consistently reproduces key molecular and cellular features of PE than prolonged hypoxia. This work establishes a framework for modelling hypoxia-induced ST dysfunction while highlighting the importance of oxygen control conditions and hypoxic exposure duration when modeling PE in vitro.

papers.title: Germ Granule Remodeling Reveals Germline Age in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Germline aging limits reproductive lifespan, yet quantitative measures of germline age at cellular resolution within intact tissue remain limited. Here, we show that two germline condensates, P granules and Mutator foci, undergo systematic age-associated remodeling in Caenorhabditis elegans, changing in morphology, spatial organization, and mutual associations. From these single-nucleus features, we develop Germ Granule Clock (GG-Clock), an image-based aging clock that accurately predicts chronological age. Intermittent fasting, a pro-longevity intervention, shifts GG-Clock predictions toward a younger germline state, demonstrating the clock's responsiveness to anti-aging interventions. To make the approach broadly usable, we introduce GGProfiler, an open-source tool that automates granule segmentation and feature extraction. Together, our findings establish germ granule architecture as an interpretable, image-based readout of germline aging and provide a platform for quantifying condensate remodeling across genetic and environmental interventions, with potential translation to other systems.

papers.title: Culture-Associated Changes in the Human Cardiac Fibroblast Surfaceome: A Proteomic Resource for Cell Surface Marker and Target Discovery
papers.abstract: Cardiac fibroblasts (CF) are central to cardiac homeostasis and fibrosis, but the lack of reliable cell surface markers limits their direct isolation, characterization, and selective targeting in human myocardium. Most CF studies use cultured cells, yet how the cell surface changes during culture remains poorly defined. We used mass spectrometry-based surfaceome profiling in five sequential substudies of human CF, spanning failing and non-failing hearts, fresh and cryopreserved myocardium, and laboratory-isolated and commercially sourced cells. Culture was associated with extensive changes in surface protein abundance, which were largest between P0 and P1 and were reproduced in CF from fresh and cryopreserved tissue. These changes included increases in proteins associated with fibroblast activation and matrix production, and changes in proteins used as CF markers and pharmacologic targets. Whole cell proteomics showed that these changes extended beyond the cell surface. Because culture history shapes cultured CF, we examined 30 years of CF literature, revealing widespread use of later, mixed, or unreported passages and incomplete reporting of culture conditions. To aid future studies, we developed CFxplorer (CFxplorer.net), an interactive resource that integrates this literature analysis, passage-resolved protein trajectories, and a Human CF Surfaceome Atlas of 1,577 cell surface N-glycoproteins detected across 234 CF samples, with extracellular peptide evidence and biological and pharmacologic annotations to help prioritize candidate surface markers and targets for validation. Collectively, this study expands the human CF surfaceome, defines how it changes during culture, and shows that the properties of cultured CF should be verified, not assumed, before use in experiments.

papers.title: mRNA/LNP-mediated expression of a ligand-independent Tie2 pathway activator, COMP-Tie2*, enables sustained endothelial stabilization
papers.abstract: Activation of the angiopoietin/Tie2 signaling axis is a validated strategy for endothelial stabilization. However, therapeutic Tie2 activation via angiopoietin-1 (Ang1) or Ang1-derived agonists is intrinsically limited due to several mechanism including ligand instability, competitive Ang2 inhibition, Tie2 ectodomain cleavage, VE-PTP-mediated Tie2 dephosphorylation, and ligand-induced receptor degradation. All these inhibitory mechanisms restrict both magnitude as well as duration of therapeutic Tie2 signaling, particularly under inflammatory conditions such as acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) or sepsis. Here, we describe a novel ligand-independent strategy for sustained Tie2 activation based on engineered membrane-anchored Tie2 variants. By combining intracellular Tie2 kinase domains harboring naturally occurring autoactivating mutations with heterologous membrane-targeting domains, we generated truncated, constitutively active Tie2 variants that bypass extracellular ligand regulation entirely. mRNA-mediated expression of these constructs induced robust and persistent Tie2 autophosphorylation and downstream Akt-FOXO1 signaling in pulmonary endothelial cells, which exceeded COMP-Ang1-mediated activation in both strength and duration. Systemic administration of COMP-Tie2* mRNA using lung-targeted lipid nanoparticles resulted in selective pulmonary Tie2 receptor engagement in vivo. Collectively, these data establish LNP-mediated mRNA delivery of engineered recombinant receptors for intrinsic Tie2 activation as a promising novel approach for endothelial stabilization under inflammatory conditions.

papers.title: Enhancing pancreatic islet cell survival via NMDAR antagonist-driven ROR1 activation as revealed by phosphoproteomics
papers.abstract: NMDA receptors (NMDARs) control function and survival not only of neurons, but also of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells. Since insufficient insulin secretion and beta cell death are key events during diabetes development, targeting NMDARs offers a therapeutic approach. Specifically, the NMDAR antagonist dextrorphan (DXO) increases glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in clinical trials. Furthermore, treatment with DXO or optimized DXO derivatives prevents pancreatic islet cell death upon diabetogenic insults. Nonetheless, the signaling pathways induced by NMDAR inhibition are poorly understood. Here, we use complementary approaches, phosphoproteomics and tyrosine kinase profiling, to demonstrate that DXO and its derivatives rapidly regulate multiple intracellular signaling clusters, including mTOR and ERK signaling, in pancreatic islets. Notably, mTOR inhibition, but not ERK inhibition, is sufficient to negate DXO's protective effects. Further, we show that activation of Receptor Tyrosine Kinase-like Orphan Receptor 1 (ROR1) is a universal event upon NMDAR inhibition in islets. Simultaneous knockdown of Ror1/ROR1 and its paralogue Ror2/ROR2 compromises the viability of both mouse and human islets, highlighting the ROR1/2 signaling axis as a promising avenue for enhancing beta cell survival.

papers.title: Evaluation of N8-propargyl spermidine as a chemical probe for deoxyhypusine synthase-dependent post-translational modifications
papers.abstract: Hypusination is a highly conserved post-translational modification generated on eukaryotic translation factor 5A (eIF5A) by the sequential action of deoxyhypusine synthase (DHS) and deoxyhypusine hydroxylase (DOHH). Recently, expanded DHS substrate specificity and DHS-dependent acetylhypusination of receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) have been proposed based on studies employing N8-propargyl spermidine in click chemistry-based workflows, alongside additional analyses. Here, we used orthogonal approaches to evaluate N8-propargyl spermidine as a chemical probe for protein hypusination and to reassess the evidence for DHS-dependent modification of RIPK1. Protein labeling following treatment of cells with the probe was unaffected by DHS inhibition but was strongly reduced when cysteines were alkylated after metabolic labeling and before initiation of the click reaction, suggesting that probe-associated adducts form through reactions involving free cysteine thiols after cell lysis. Consistent with this observation, analysis of probe-modified peptides localized adducts to cysteine residues, with masses consistent with copper-dependent azide-alkyne-thiol coupling, and detected no lysine modifications corresponding to propargylated hypusine or deoxyhypusine. In a reconstituted enzymatic assay, N8-propargyl spermidine did not support DHS-dependent modification of eIF5A, whereas native spermidine supported robust modification of eIF5A but no detectable modification of RIPK1. Furthermore, our structural study revealed a non-productive binding mode of N8-propargyl spermidine to DHS. These findings challenge the interpretation of widespread chemical probe-derived labeling as evidence for expanded DHS substrate specificity and highlight the need for stringent validation before proposing new hypusination targets.

papers.title: Comprehensive engineering of the CasX-Editor to generate a therapeutically optimized genome editor
papers.abstract: CRISPR-based genetic modification is enabling curative, one-time treatments, but extending its use to more diseases will require increasing potency at low doses while avoiding unintended genomic modification. CRISPR technologies derive from microbial nucleases, such as Cas9, whose properties evolved for antiviral defense rather than precision editing in human cells. Although these systems can be engineered for greater activity or specificity, improving both properties to meet the challenges of in vivo delivery in large animals remains challenging. Here we used iterative molecular engineering of the Cas12e protein and its guide RNA to produce the X-Editor (XE), a compact nuclease platform that combines robust in vivo activity with exceptional genomic specificity. Screening tens of thousands of protein variants and guide designs and iteratively testing and combining beneficial mutations yielded an enzyme with more than 100-fold higher editing activity in human cells. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed novel inter- and intramolecular interactions driving enhanced function. XE mRNA was delivered to nonhuman primate liver via lipid nanoparticle with guides for two distinct targets. At both targets, XE demonstrated greater editing at lower doses than comparable preclinical data from Cas9-based therapies that are now in clinical testing. No off-target editing was detected for either guide in full specificity assessments performed in primary human hepatocytes at doses tenfold above the on-target effective concentration (EC90). These findings establish that more potent in vivo editing and stringent genomic specificity can be jointly engineered into a naturally compact CRISPR system for delivery using adeno-associated virus (AAV) or lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery strategies. These results provide a new foundation for advanced genetic medicines that demand lower dosing and greatly reduced off-target risk.
